source(onet2r_inst_path(

Two occupations can share reading, communication, and problem solving yet
differ in what they produce or the knowledge they need. I want to understand
those differences without making every shared requirement disappear into
a broad label.

I start with a simpler question. Which recorded activities appear in many
occupations, and which appear in only a few? TF-IDF gives uncommon links
more weight. For a binary activity list, an occupation's summary is the
mean log inverse prevalence of its activities.

Rarity alone leaves a lot unanswered. Two occupations might share the same
unusual activities and be each other's closest neighbor. A common skill
could distinguish them through its required level. I therefore compare
profiles as well as rarity, and check what changes when labels, occupation
weights or distance rules change.

The information-loss budget asks how much a listed activity tells us about
which occupation it came from, and how much of that information remains
after grouping the labels. It is a calculation about descriptions.
Economic value, worker time and effects of AI need evidence these records
do not contain.

The article uses a **derived snapshot of the full public O&#42;NET 30.3
archive** and clearly labeled **stylized examples** to explain the formulas.
Article builds use bundled tables and do not access the network.
The helpers are article code, not exported package functions or an endorsed
substantive score. Rankings describe the covered O&#42;NET occupations under
the specified choices, not all jobs or workers in the United States.

```{r snapshot-data, include = FALSE}
read_snapshot <- function(name) {

    onet2r_inst_path("extdata", "occupational-distinctiveness", name),

}
observed_prevalence <- read_snapshot("activity-prevalence.csv")

  tibble::as_tibble(utils::read.csv(
    snapshot_csv_path(file.path(
      onet2r_inst_path("extdata", "occupational-extensions"), paste0(name, ".csv")
    )),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE, na.strings = c("NA", "")
  ))
}
employment_coverage <- read_extension("employment-coverage")
employment_prevalence <- read_extension("activity-employment-prevalence")
employment_summary <- read_extension("activity-employment-summary")
skill_distributions <- read_extension("skills-rating-distributions")
skill_sensitivity <- read_extension("skills-neighbor-sensitivity")
skill_gaps <- read_extension("skills-pair-gap-examples")
skill_anchors <- read_extension("skills-level-anchors")
cross_summary <- read_extension("cross-domain-overlap-summary")
cross_selected <- read_extension("cross-domain-selected-neighbors")
software_tied_k5 <- read_extension("cross-domain-neighbors") |>
  filter(block == "software", rank <= 5L) |>
  count(occupation) |>
  summarise(n_tied = sum(n > 5L)) |>
  pull(n_tied)
block_labels <- c(
  dwa = "Activities", software = "Software",
  es_im = "Essential: Importance", es_lv = "Essential: Level",
  ts_im = "Transferable: Importance", ts_lv = "Transferable: Level"
)
employment_display <- employment_prevalence |>
  filter(unit_rule == "soc") |>
  left_join(observed_prevalence |> select(item, dwa_element_name),
            by = c("dwa_element_id" = "item"), relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  arrange(desc(prevalence_employment), dwa_element_id) |>
  slice_head(n = 8)
observed_occupations <- read_snapshot("occupation-profiles.csv")
observed_coverage <- read_snapshot("coverage.csv")
snapshot <- read_snapshot("provenance.csv")
observed_resolution <- read_snapshot("resolution-summary.csv")
information_summary <- read_snapshot("information-summary.csv")
information_loss <- read_snapshot("information-loss.csv")
information_diagnostics <- read_snapshot("information-occupation-diagnostics.csv")
random_hierarchy <- read_snapshot("information-random-hierarchy.csv")
null_summary <- read_snapshot("null-summary.csv")
group_weighting <- read_snapshot("group-weighting-sensitivity.csv")
base_figures <- distinctiveness_figures(
  observed_prevalence, observed_occupations,
  observed_resolution
)
audit_figures <- distinctiveness_audit_figures(
  information_summary, information_loss, null_summary, random_hierarchy
)
observed_occupations$size_band <- cut(
  observed_occupations$n_activities, c(0, 10, 20, 30, Inf),
  labels = c("5 to 10", "11 to 20", "21 to 30", "31 or more")
)
size_rho <- stats::cor(
  observed_occupations$n_activities, observed_occupations$mean_idf,
  method = "spearman"
)
size_nearest_rho <- stats::cor(
  observed_occupations$n_activities, observed_occupations$nearest_distance,
  method = "spearman"
)
rarity_nearest_rho <- stats::cor(
  observed_occupations$mean_idf, observed_occupations$nearest_distance,
  method = "spearman"
)
group_weighting_rho <- stats::cor(
  group_weighting$rarity_rank,
  group_weighting$prefix5_weighted_rank,
  method = "spearman"
)
top_ten_weighting_overlap <- length(intersect(
  group_weighting$occupation[group_weighting$rarity_rank <= 10L],
  group_weighting$occupation[group_weighting$prefix5_weighted_rank <= 10L]
))
identical_profile_rows <- observed_occupations |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$nearest_distance == 0)
identical_profile_pairs <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(
  seq_len(nrow(identical_profile_rows)),
  function(i) {
    occupation <- identical_profile_rows$occupation[[i]]
    neighbors <- strsplit(
      identical_profile_rows$nearest_occupations[[i]], ";", fixed = TRUE
    )[[1]]
    tibble::tibble(
      occupation_a = pmin(occupation, neighbors),
      occupation_b = pmax(occupation, neighbors)
    )
  }
)) |>
  dplyr::distinct(.data$occupation_a, .data$occupation_b) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    prefix5_a = substr(.data$occupation_a, 1, 5),
    prefix5_b = substr(.data$occupation_b, 1, 5),
    same_prefix5 = .data$prefix5_a == .data$prefix5_b,
    same_major_group = substr(.data$occupation_a, 1, 2) ==
      substr(.data$occupation_b, 1, 2),
    occupation_a_title = observed_occupations$title[
      match(.data$occupation_a, observed_occupations$occupation)
    ],
    occupation_b_title = observed_occupations$title[
      match(.data$occupation_b, observed_occupations$occupation)
    ]
  )
stopifnot(
  nrow(identical_profile_pairs) == 5L,
  all(identical_profile_pairs$same_major_group)
)
```

## First choose a shared unit of work

Treat an occupation as a document and a shared activity as a term. Do not start
by treating occupation-specific Task IDs as a universal task vocabulary. Count
their actual cross-occupation overlap first. If almost every ID belongs to only
one occupation, almost every ID receives the same rarity weight.

O&#42;NET provides a more useful bridge: **Tasks to DWAs** links task statements
to Detailed Work Activities. The **GWAs to IWAs to DWAs** reference supplies
the hierarchy from detailed to intermediate to generalized activities. These
links provide a published shared vocabulary without requiring an embedding
model or treating different wording as different work.

The next example uses the bundled miniature fixture, with two occupations. It
demonstrates the join only; the full-archive results begin below.

```{r archive-links}
archive_dir <- onet2r_inst_path("extdata", "onet-mini", "db_30_3_text")
tasks <- onet_archive_read(
  "30.3", "Task Statements", path = archive_dir,
  release_date = "2026-05-01"
)
links <- onet_archive_read(
  "30.3", "Tasks to DWAs", path = archive_dir,
  release_date = "2026-05-01"
)
hierarchy <- onet_archive_reference(
  "30.3", "GWAs to IWAs to DWAs", path = archive_dir,
  release_date = "2026-05-01"
)

task_overlap <- tasks |>
  distinct(onet_soc_code, task_id) |>
  count(task_id, name = "n_occupations")
task_overlap |>
  count(n_occupations, name = "n_task_ids") |>
  knitr::kable()

dwa_names <- hierarchy |>
  distinct(dwa_element_id, dwa_element_name)
activity_links <- links |>
  select(onet_soc_code, task_id, dwa_element_id) |>
  distinct() |>
  left_join(dwa_names, by = "dwa_element_id", relationship = "many-to-one")
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(activity_links$dwa_element_id),
  !anyNA(activity_links$dwa_element_name)
)
activity_links |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Use the reference join even if the miniature fixture already includes names.
Real text archives omit repeated labels from the link files. For a full
archive, join occupation titles from `Occupation Data` and task text from
`Task Statements`, using occupation plus Task ID for the latter.

Before scoring, report the number of occupations with task statements, with
links, and with usable ratings, plus the share of tasks that have a DWA link.
Inspect unmapped tasks and suppressed ratings. **An unobserved profile is not a
zero-work occupation.** The helpers below reject missing or all-zero occupation
profiles rather than silently shrink the declared universe.

## Define frequency, prevalence, and distinctiveness separately

Let \(x_{od}\) be a non-negative activity weight for occupation \(o\) and
activity \(d\), and let \(N\) be the number of occupations in a fixed universe.
The baseline uses binary presence: \(x_{od}=1\) if at least one retained task
links to the activity, and zero otherwise.

\[
df_d = \sum_o \mathbf{1}(x_{od}>0)
\]
\[
prevalence_d = df_d/N
\]
\[
tf_{od} = \frac{x_{od}}{\sum_j x_{oj}}
\]
\[
idf_d = \log(N/df_d)
\]
\[
tfidf_{od} = tf_{od}\,idf_d
\]

Here TF means **within-occupation profile share**, not work time. Count each
occupation once in document frequency, regardless of how many of its tasks map
to the activity. The unsmoothed IDF deliberately assigns zero to a universally
present activity. A convention such as \(1+\log((N+1)/(df_d+1))\) would not.

For an occupation-level rarity summary, use
\(D_o=\sum_d tfidf_{od}\). It is the average log inverse prevalence of that
occupation's activity profile. Retain the item-level contributions so the
score remains interpretable.

## What the full archive shows

The snapshot covers **`r snapshot$n_linked_occupations` occupations** with
`r snapshot$n_tasks` task statements and `r snapshot$n_activities` linked DWAs.
All `r snapshot$n_linked_tasks` task statements have at least one DWA link.
The occupation taxonomy contains `r snapshot$n_taxonomy_occupations` entries,
so `r snapshot$n_taxonomy_occupations - snapshot$n_linked_occupations` entries
are outside this task-based analytic universe. We do not give them zero scores.
There are `r snapshot$n_shared_task_ids` Task IDs shared across occupations,
which is why shared activities are a more useful baseline vocabulary.

The baseline retains any linked task, including Supplemental tasks, counts each
occupation-DWA link once, and gives each occupation equal weight. Task ratings,
employment weights, and AI-exposure measures are excluded.

Four properties of this archive limit what the rankings can mean.

- **Presence is cheap.** One linked task, even a Supplemental one, makes an
  occupation-DWA pair present. Occupations have 4 to 40 task statements and 5
  to 41 DWAs. Slaughterers and Meat Packers has 14 task statements, all
  Supplemental and none Core. Models has ten, one Core and nine Supplemental.
  Restricting the data literally to Core tasks would shrink the universe to 893
  occupations and make Models a one-DWA rarity leader. That is a different
  universe, not a robustness pass on this ranking.
- **Measurement dates differ.** Task vintages span 2004 to 2025 inside the May
  2026 archive. The release is not a uniform 2026 measurement.
- **Rankings are summaries of database labels.** They describe one published
  archive. They are not estimates of a population quantity, so they come with
  no confidence intervals and no sampling interpretation.
- **Code granularity matters.** The baseline gives every O&#42;NET-SOC code
  equal weight. A code group with more detailed codes therefore contributes
  more total weight to activity prevalence than a group with fewer codes. The
  results are code-weighted comparisons, not equally weighted comparisons of
  occupational families.

### Most common and least common detailed activities

```{r observed-common}
observed_prevalence |>
  slice_max(n_occupations, n = 8, with_ties = TRUE) |>
  select(dwa_element_name, n_occupations, prevalence) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c(
    "Detailed work activity", "Occupations", "Share of covered occupations"
  ))
```

```{r figure-common, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "The eight most widely linked detailed work activities, with the number and share of the 923 covered occupations.", fig.alt = "Horizontal bar chart of the eight DWAs linked to the most occupations. The largest is linked to 91 of 923 occupations, about 9.9 percent. The table above gives the exact values."}
base_figures$common
```

The most widely linked DWA is **`r observed_prevalence$dwa_element_name[[1]]`**
It appears in `r observed_prevalence$n_occupations[[1]]` of
`r snapshot$n_linked_occupations` covered occupations, or
`r round(100 * observed_prevalence$prevalence[[1]], 1)` percent.
"Most common" is therefore relative: these are quite specific activity
descriptions, not a complete inventory of general human capabilities.

At the other end, **`r sum(observed_prevalence$n_occupations == 1L)` DWAs occur
in only one covered occupation**. They tie on document frequency and IDF.
The next table shows eight of these tied activities in identifier order, not
eight uniquely lowest-ranked activities.

```{r observed-uncommon}
observed_prevalence |>
  filter(n_occupations == 1L) |>
  arrange(item) |>
  head(8) |>
  select(dwa_element_name, n_occupations) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Example singleton DWA", "Occupations"))
```

### Occupations with the rarest activity profiles

```{r observed-rarity}
observed_occupations |>
  slice_min(rarity_rank, n = 8, with_ties = TRUE) |>
  select(rarity_rank, title, n_activities, mean_idf, nearest_distance) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c(
    "Rank", "Occupation", "DWAs", "Mean IDF", "Nearest profile distance"
  ))
```

**`r observed_occupations$title[[1]]` ranks first on this particular rarity
summary**, with `r observed_occupations$n_activities[[1]]` linked activities,
the smallest profile size in the archive, a minimum shared by six occupations. Its fourteen statements are all
Supplemental, so its rank rests on labels attached to non-Core tasks. It is not
necessarily the most isolated occupation, the most specialized occupation under
another vocabulary, or the occupation with the largest entry barriers.

Profile size matters. With binary profiles, the score is a mean over
\(n_o\) activities, so small profiles have more variable scores. In this
archive, profile size and the rarity score have a Spearman correlation of
`r round(size_rho, 2)`, and profile size and nearest-neighbor distance have
`r round(size_nearest_rho, 2)`. Read the rankings with the DWA counts beside
them, as in the table above.

These observations are a descriptive starting point. A publishable substantive
claim should survive Core-only filtering, alternative task-link weights,
minimum-coverage restrictions, and broader activity groupings. The snapshot
does not claim those robustness checks have all been passed. Snapshot rarity
scores and distances are rounded to 12 decimal places before ranking or choosing
neighbors so numerical noise does not break ties.

### Sensitivity to occupational-code granularity

The baseline gives each of the 923 detailed O&#42;NET-SOC codes equal weight.
As a sensitivity, this calculation first finds each DWA's prevalence within
each five-character code-prefix group, then averages those prevalences
with each represented prefix group receiving equal weight:

\[
\bar p_d = \frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}
\frac{\text{codes in }g\text{ linked to }d}
{\text{covered codes in }g}.
\]
\[
\mathrm{IDF}^{*}_d = \log(1/\bar p_d).
\]

The within-occupation TF remains normalized as before. This changes the
reference prevalence, not the occupational activity profiles. The two rankings
have a Spearman correlation of `r round(group_weighting_rho, 2)`, and
`r top_ten_weighting_overlap` occupations ranked in the top ten (including
ties) overlap.

```{r figure-group-weighting, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Occupation rarity ranks under equal detailed-code weights versus equal five-character code-group weights. Points away from the diagonal change rank when the prevalence denominator changes.", fig.alt = "Scatter plot comparing each of 923 occupations' rarity rank under equal code weights with its rank when five-character code-prefix groups receive equal weight. The diagonal indicates unchanged rank; a table below lists occupations with the largest shifts."}
ggplot2::ggplot(
  group_weighting,
  ggplot2::aes(
    x = .data$rarity_rank, y = .data$prefix5_weighted_rank
  )
) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(
    slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
    color = onet2r_colors[["gray"]]
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    color = onet2r_colors[["slate"]], alpha = 0.35, size = 1.5
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_reverse() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Equal code-group weights change some rarity ranks",
    subtitle = "The activity profiles are unchanged; only prevalence weights differ",
    x = "Rank with equal weight per detailed occupation code",
    y = "Rank with equal weight per five-character code group",
    caption = "Rank 1 is highest. This is a weighting sensitivity, not a preferred occupational taxonomy."
  ) +
  onet2r_theme(base_size = 16)
```

```{r group-weighting-table, echo = FALSE}
group_weighting |>
  slice_max(abs(rank_change), n = 8, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(rank_change)), occupation) |>
  mutate(occupation_label = paste0(title, " (", soc_prefix5, ")")) |>
  select(
    occupation_label, rarity_rank, prefix5_weighted_rank, rank_change
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c(
    "Occupation (code prefix)", "Code-weighted rank",
    "Group-weighted rank", "Rank change"
  ))
```

These prefix groups are not the official SOC minor groups. The employment
extension below also uses the actual minor-group definition and reports the
two grouping choices separately.

This sensitivity gives each represented prefix group equal influence on DWA
prevalence; it does not make the group definitions substantively neutral.
Different taxonomies or broader grouping levels could produce different
rankings. The baseline remains the primary result because it is the declared
equal-code comparison, not because it is invariant to taxonomy granularity.
Positive rank changes indicate a better numeric rank under the group-weighted
sensitivity; negative values indicate a worse rank.

### Skeptical check: profile size

```{r size-table, echo = FALSE}
observed_occupations |>
  summarise(
    occupations = n(), mean_rarity = mean(mean_idf),
    mean_nearest_distance = mean(nearest_distance),
    .by = size_band
  ) |>
  arrange(size_band) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c(
    "DWAs in profile", "Occupations", "Mean rarity score",
    "Mean nearest distance"
  ))
```

```{r figure-inventory-size, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Real O*NET 30.3: rarity score against number of linked DWAs, with the rarity leader labeled.", fig.alt = "Scatter plot of 923 occupations with number of linked detailed work activities on the horizontal axis and rarity score on the vertical axis. The rarity score tends to be lower for larger profiles, with a Spearman correlation of about minus 0.29, and the scores spread more widely at small profile sizes."}
base_figures$inventory_size
```

## Work through the score on a stylized example

```{r stylized-activities}
activity_labels <- tibble::tribble(
  ~item, ~activity, ~broad_group,
  "communicate", "Exchange information", "Interaction",
  "analyze", "Analyze evidence", "Information",
  "test", "Test a system", "Information",
  "report", "Prepare a technical report", "Information",
  "care", "Provide direct care", "Practical work",
  "diagnose", "Diagnose a condition", "Information",
  "safety", "Check safety conditions", "Practical work",
  "repair", "Repair equipment", "Practical work",
  "teach", "Teach a procedure", "Interaction"
)
activity_sets <- list(
  A = c("communicate", "analyze", "test"),
  B = c("communicate", "analyze", "report"),
  C = c("communicate", "care", "diagnose"),
  D = c("communicate", "care", "safety"),
  E = c("communicate", "repair", "safety"),
  F = c("communicate", "teach", "report")
)
universe <- names(activity_sets)
activity_profiles <- bind_rows(lapply(universe, function(code) {
  tibble::tibble(occupation = code, item = activity_sets[[code]], weight = 1)
}))
scores <- profile_tfidf(activity_profiles, universe)

prevalence_table <- scores |>
  distinct(item, n_occupations, prevalence, idf) |>
  left_join(activity_labels, by = "item", relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  arrange(desc(prevalence), activity)
prevalence_table |>
  select(activity, n_occupations, prevalence, idf) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

"Exchange information" appears in all six stylized occupations and receives
zero IDF. "Test a system" appears in one and receives \(\log(6)\). Neither
statement establishes that testing is more important than communication.

```{r distinctive-occupations}
rarity <- scores |>
  summarise(mean_idf = sum(tf_idf), .by = occupation) |>
  mutate(rarity_rank = min_rank(desc(mean_idf))) |>
  arrange(rarity_rank, occupation)
rarity |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

scores |>
  left_join(activity_labels, by = "item", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  filter(occupation == "A") |>
  arrange(desc(tf_idf), activity) |>
  select(occupation, activity, share, idf, tf_idf) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Keep ties rather than declaring an arbitrary winner. A national ranking and a
ranking within healthcare answer different questions because the denominator
and IDF change. If the question is whether two groups differ, calculate their
scores with the **same vocabulary and reference IDF**, not separately fitted
IDFs that place each group on its own scale.

### Alternative weights need their own interpretation

Binary presence avoids rewarding occupations merely because they have more
task statements. As sensitivity checks, use distinct linked-task counts or
task Importance/Relevance weights. A task can map to several DWAs. For a
count- or rating-weighted profile, split its mass over its \(k\) retained links
as \(w_t/k\), then sum by occupation and DWA. Otherwise heavily mapped tasks
receive more total weight just because they have more links.

Decide whether to retain Supplemental tasks before calculating \(k\).
Audit missing ratings instead of dropping them through an inner join. Relevance,
Importance, and frequency-category responses are different quantities.
Multiplying them does not produce an observed share of working hours.

## Rare activities and unusual occupations are not the same

To identify unusual *combinations*, compare whole profiles. Here the distance
between two normalized profiles is total variation:

\[
TV(o,p) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_d |tf_{od}-tf_{pd}|.
\]

It ranges from zero for identical compositions to one for disjoint profiles.
Using the original shares preserves ubiquitous activities that TF-IDF would
erase. Cosine similarity is another defensible choice, but a profile containing
only universal activities has a zero TF-IDF vector and no defined TF-IDF cosine.

```{r nearest-neighbor}
activity_distances <- profile_distances(activity_profiles, universe)
directed_distances <- bind_rows(
  activity_distances |>
    transmute(occupation = occupation_a, neighbor = occupation_b, distance),
  activity_distances |>
    transmute(occupation = occupation_b, neighbor = occupation_a, distance)
)
nearest <- directed_distances |>
  group_by(occupation) |>
  slice_min(distance, with_ties = TRUE) |>
  ungroup()
nearest |>
  left_join(rarity, by = "occupation", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  arrange(desc(distance), occupation, neighbor) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The nearest-neighbor distance measures isolation: how far an occupation sits
from its closest profile. Do not add the average distance to all occupations as
a second atypicality score. With about two thousand mostly sparse activities,
almost every pair of profiles is nearly disjoint, so each occupation's average
distance is close to one and tracks the rarity score (a Spearman correlation of
about 0.88 in this archive). Inspect the nearest neighbors and activity
contributions rather than relying on one rank. Neither rarity nor distance
establishes that workers can readily move between two occupations.

For binary profiles of sizes \(a\) and \(b\) that share \(k\) activities, total
variation has the closed form \(TV = 1 - k/\max(a,b)\). It depends on the
overlap count and the larger profile size, and it ignores how rare the shared
activities are. That is why rarity and isolation can disagree, and why
isolation carries a profile-size dependence of its own: a small profile is
close to another only if that profile is also small and shares most of its
activities; full containment in a larger profile still leaves a large
distance. The example above is **stylized**; the table below uses the real
archive.

For comparison, the most isolated full-archive profiles under this same
binary-presence, unweighted total-variation rule are:

```{r observed-isolation}
observed_occupations |>
  slice_max(nearest_distance, n = 8, with_ties = TRUE) |>
  arrange(desc(nearest_distance), occupation) |>
  select(title, n_activities, nearest_distance, rarity_rank) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c(
    "Occupation", "DWAs", "Nearest distance", "Rarity rank"
  ))
```

```{r figure-rarity-isolation, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Real O*NET 30.3 occupations: rarity score against nearest-neighbor total-variation distance, with the rarity leader and the most isolated profile labeled.", fig.alt = "Scatter plot of 923 occupations. Rarity score is on the horizontal axis and nearest-neighbor distance on the vertical axis. The two are only weakly related, with a Spearman correlation of about 0.36. The tables above and below give exact values."}
base_figures$rarity_isolation
```

```{r rarity-isolation-table, echo = FALSE}
observed_occupations |>
  filter(rarity_rank == 1L | nearest_distance == max(nearest_distance)) |>
  select(title, n_activities, mean_idf, nearest_distance, rarity_rank) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c(
    "Labeled occupation", "DWAs", "Mean IDF", "Nearest distance", "Rarity rank"
  ))
```

The rank correlation between mean IDF and nearest-profile distance is
`r round(rarity_nearest_rho, 2)`. The different ordering is useful evidence
that item rarity and isolation answer different questions. Distances are
descriptive distances between published activity profiles, not probabilities
of successful job transitions.

The snapshot also contains `r nrow(identical_profile_pairs)` pairs with exactly
the same detailed activity set. All five share O&#42;NET-SOC major-group prefix
25, but `r sum(!identical_profile_pairs$same_prefix5)` pairs cross five-character
code-group prefixes. Detailed codes can therefore distinguish labels even when
their linked DWA inventories are identical; this small cluster does not show
that all occupations within a major group share the same work.

```{r identical-profile-table, echo = FALSE}
identical_profile_pairs |>
  mutate(
    occupation_a_label = paste(occupation_a, occupation_a_title, sep = ": "),
    occupation_b_label = paste(occupation_b, occupation_b_title, sep = ": "),
    code_prefixes = paste(
      prefix5_a, prefix5_b, sep = " / "
    )
  ) |>
  select(occupation_a_label, occupation_b_label, code_prefixes) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c(
    "Occupation A", "Occupation B", "Five-character prefixes (A / B)"
  ))
```

## What changes when larger occupations count more?

An activity can appear in few occupation codes but still be attached to a
large amount of employment. To examine that, I pair the 30.3 descriptions
with the May 2025 national OEWS estimates. This changes the reference
population. It does not tell us how often workers perform the activity.

The mapping needs more care than matching the first six digits. OEWS
publishes some occupations as combined cells. O&#42;NET also has broad
`.00` descriptions alongside narrower specialties. Those descriptions
cannot all be treated as separate groups of workers.

The primary comparison therefore uses one `.00` description per constituent
SOC occupation. A cell enters the point estimate only if every expected
description is available. I do not fill a missing broad description with a
specialty profile. For a combined cell, the point estimate divides its
employment equally among its constituent SOC descriptions. That split is
an assumption, not a published employment breakdown.

```{r employment-coverage-table, echo = FALSE}
employment_coverage |>
  filter(unit_rule == "soc",
         scope %in% c("official_total", "returned_panel", "complete",
                      "partial", "no_profile", "official_not_returned")) |>
  select(scope, n_cells, employment, share_official_total) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 0, 0, 4), col.names = c(
    "Scope", "Published cells", "Employment", "Share of official total"
  ))
```

The complete cells cover 146.25 million jobs, or 94.1 percent of the
release's official total. Another 9.23 million are in cells with incomplete
descriptions. Separately, the sum of the 830 returned detailed cells falls
13,890 below the official total. I leave that difference unexplained rather
than allocate it to an activity.

OEWS covers nonfarm wage-and-salary employment, not all workers. In
particular, these estimates exclude the self-employed and the military.
The results below are conditional on the complete cells, not estimates of
activity use across the entire workforce.

For a binary activity link, employment-weighted prevalence and the share of
allocated employment attached to a linked description are the same
calculation. If \(E_s\) is a cell's employment, \(a_{os}\) its assumed
within-cell allocation, and \(z_{od}\) a description's activity link:

\[
P_d = \frac{\sum_s E_s\sum_o a_{os}z_{od}}{\sum_s E_s}.
\]

The table compares this with equal-description prevalence on the same
765-description support. Official SOC minor groups receive equal weight
in another sensitivity. The older five-character-prefix grouping is kept
separately.

```{r employment-prevalence, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "The eight activities with the largest employment-allocated prevalence in the complete-cell comparison. Both series use the same SOC-description support.", fig.alt = "Paired points compare equal-description prevalence with employment-allocated prevalence for eight activities. The connecting lines show how the choice of weights changes prevalence; the table below supplies both values and the allocation bounds."}
employment_prevalence_figure(employment_display)
```

```{r employment-prevalence-table, echo = FALSE}
employment_display |>
  transmute(
    Activity = dwa_element_name,
    `Equal descriptions (%)` = 100 * prevalence_equal_unit,
    `Employment allocation (%)` = 100 * prevalence_employment,
    `Allocation lower (%)` = 100 * employment_lower,
    `Allocation upper (%)` = 100 * employment_upper
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

Across activities, the equal-description and employment-weighted prevalence
orders have a Spearman correlation of about 0.66. Recomputing IDF from the
employment prevalence changes the rarity order too. It answers how unusual
a link is against this allocated employment distribution. Averaging the
original rarity scores with employment weights would be a different operation.

For each complete cell, I also let its employment fall anywhere among the
constituent SOC descriptions. The smallest and largest possible link shares
give the allocation bounds above. Among the 2,034 DWAs linked to these
descriptions, 92.4 percent have zero-width bounds. This says that most links are unaffected
by the remaining within-cell split. It does not settle the missing cells:
the wider bounds in the bundled table let each incomplete cell's link be
either zero or one, relative to returned-panel employment.

These are allocation bounds, not confidence intervals. They do not include
OEWS sampling error or turn recorded links into worker behavior. A separate
all-code sensitivity reweights overlapping `.00` and specialty descriptions.
Its min/max results are labeled a **profile envelope**, not a sharp bound
over disjoint groups of workers.

The raw-file audit also matters. All twelve published combination codes
already have detailed rows in this year's file. Seven appear again as
broad rows with the same employment. Adding those broad rows would double
count them; the existing detailed-row filter is appropriate for these inputs.

## Skills, knowledge, experience, and working conditions

Use a separate representation for each domain:

| Domain | Useful representation | What not to do |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Detailed work activities | Binary presence or an explicit task-link weighting rule | Count occupation-specific wording as shared activity without checking |
| Software examples | Deduplicated exact-name links, with separate classification-level views | Treat listed examples or posting flags as worker-use rates |
| Skills, knowledge, abilities | One declared Importance or Level scale per element | Treat every recorded positive rating as a meaningful presence indicator |
| Related experience and training | Full response distribution within each element and scale | Treat category codes as years or pool unrelated category systems |
| Work context | Scale-aware ratings or category distributions | Mix all contexts and scales as interchangeable units |
| Education and Job Zone | Separate entry-requirement descriptors | Interpret a summary category as the full requirement profile |

In release 30.3 the dictionary lists **Essential Skills**, **Transferable
Skills**, **Education**, and **Training and Experience** separately. Do not
assume an older filename such as `Skills` or `Education, Training, and
Experience` applies to this release.

Many rated descriptors appear for almost every occupation. Binary IDF then
collapses toward zero even when required *levels* differ substantially. A
threshold such as Importance above a chosen cutoff creates a prevalence
measure, but the cutoff is a research choice that needs sensitivity checks.
Keep raw levels and their element-specific anchors alongside any normalized
profile. Normalizing ratings removes overall intensity and treats rating
values as comparable non-negative weights, an assumption rather than a property
of an ordinal scale.

For experience, O&#42;NET's category percentages describe respondents' answers
about requirements. They are **not** the distribution of actual tenure among
workers. Related Work Experience (`RW`), On-Site or In-Plant Training (`PT`),
and On-The-Job Training (`OJ`) each require their own category lookup.

Total variation ignores the ordering of experience bins. If distance in required
duration matters, use an ordered-distribution distance with justified category
locations and explicit treatment of open-ended categories. Do not assign
arbitrary midpoints and call the result measured years of experience.

We keep these domains separate rather than average them into one score.
Giving each block an equal weight would still be a judgment about what
matters, and putting all the columns in one vector would give longer
questionnaires more influence. Neither choice follows from the data.

Normalizing ratings can also remove a difference we care about. Two profiles
with ratings `(2, 2)` and `(4, 4)` have identical shares even though every
rating differs. The skills extension therefore keeps absolute rating gaps.
Education, experience, knowledge and work context remain separate possible
extensions. This article does not combine their category systems or treat an
education requirement as a measure of the work being done.

### What the actual skills ratings show

The 30.3 files contain ten Essential Skills and 25 Transferable Skills,
each on Importance and Level scales. I analyze those four blocks separately.
Importance runs from 1 to 5; Level runs from 0 to 7 and has element-specific
anchors. The numerical ranges do not make a one-point change in Science
the same substantive change as a one-point change in Speaking.

Of the 923 activity codes, 894 have complete skill profiles. Removing the
71 with at least one Recommend Suppress flag leaves 823 for the primary
comparison. This is a meaningful restriction: Accountants and Auditors and
Software Developers are among the excluded codes. The software article's
923-code results are therefore not this common-support comparison.

Not Relevant is handled separately. I retain the recorded values rather than
turn the flag into a zero. The sensitivity tables show what changes when
flagged Level values are placed at the scale floor, and when all 894 complete
profiles are retained.

```{r skill-distributions, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Essential Skills Importance distributions across the 823 primary occupation profiles. The lines describe the spread across occupations, not uncertainty in an estimated mean.", fig.alt = "Each of ten Essential Skills has a median point and a line from the 10th to 90th percentile of Importance ratings across 823 occupations. The table below gives those values on the 1-to-5 scale."}
skill_distribution_figure(skill_distributions)
```

```{r skill-distributions-table, echo = FALSE}
skill_distributions |>
  filter(block == "es_im") |>
  select(element_name, p10, median, p90) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, col.names = c(
    "Essential skill", "10th percentile", "Median", "90th percentile"
  ))
```

Every retained rating is an eight-analyst mean in these files. A threshold
on that mean is not a count of analysts choosing a response category.
For Reading Comprehension, changing the threshold from 2 to 4 changes
how widespread the stated requirement looks:

```{r skill-threshold-example, echo = FALSE}
read_extension("skills-thresholds") |>
  filter(block == "es_im", element_name == "Reading Comprehension",
         threshold %in% c(2, 3, 4)) |>
  transmute(
    `Importance mean at least` = threshold,
    `Scale label at threshold` = threshold_label,
    `Share of primary codes (%)` = 100 * share_at_or_above
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

For profile comparisons, the primary distance is the mean absolute
element-level rating gap, divided by four for Importance or seven for Level.
Unlike row-normalized shares, this preserves overall rating differences.
It assumes comparable numerical gaps across elements within a block.

The largest Essential-Level pair gap in this primary universe is between
Physicists and Slaughterers and Meat Packers. The three largest element
gaps make the comparison less abstract:

```{r skill-gap-example, echo = FALSE}
skill_gaps |>
  filter(block == "es_lv", pair_kind == "farthest_pair") |>
  arrange(desc(gap), element_id) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  select(element_name, value_a, value_b, gap) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, col.names = c(
    "Essential skill", "Physicists: Level", "Slaughterers: Level", "Gap"
  ))
```

For context, the Reading Comprehension Level anchors run from reading
step-by-step form instructions at 2 to reading a scientific journal article
about surgical procedures at 6. Those examples help interpret a rating;
they do not make every element's scale interchangeable.

I also rank occupations within each skill element and compare percentile
profiles. That drops the equal-interval assumption about the original
ratings, although averaging percentile gaps still imposes a geometry.
The single nearest neighbor often changes:

```{r skills-ordinal-sensitivity, echo = FALSE}
skill_sensitivity |>
  filter(alternative == "ordinal_percentile",
         metric == "mean_jaccard", k %in% c(1, 5, 10)) |>
  summarise(
    k1 = value[k == 1L], k5 = value[k == 5L], k10 = value[k == 10L],
    .by = block
  ) |>
  transmute(Block = unname(block_labels[block]), k1, k5, k10) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, col.names = c(
    "Skill block", "One-neighbor overlap", "Five-neighbor overlap",
    "Ten-neighbor overlap"
  ))
```

About 48 to 55 percent of occupations have disjoint single-neighbor sets
under the absolute-gap and percentile comparisons. At five neighbors,
fewer than one percent do. The broad distance ordering is much more
stable than the identity of one nearest occupation. That is a reason to
show neighborhoods and element gaps rather than present one match as
definitive. These are descriptive comparisons, without significance claims
or joint confidence intervals assembled from marginal standard errors.

## Do activities, skills and software point to the same neighbors?

On the same 823 codes, I recompute activity and exact-name software distances
and compare them with each skill block. All six use the same candidate
occupations. Boundary ties are retained, after rounding distances to eight
decimal places. A five-neighbor set can therefore contain more than five
codes.

For software, `r software_tied_k5` of the 823 codes have more than five
neighbors at this cutoff. These larger tied sets also affect the overlap
comparison.

Agreement is low. At five neighbors, 55.8 percent of activity/software
comparisons share no neighbor at all. The median neighbor-set overlap is
zero. It is also zero between software and each skill block. This does
not establish that one domain is better. They record different aspects
of occupations, and the result also depends on each domain's distance rule.

```{r cross-domain-agreement, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Median neighbor-set Jaccard overlap on the common 823-code universe, with five nearest neighbors and boundary ties. Diagonal entries compare a block with itself.", fig.alt = "A six-by-six matrix compares activities, software, and four skill blocks. Median five-neighbor overlap is zero for activities versus software and for software versus every skill block. Essential Importance versus Level is 0.11; Transferable Importance versus Level is 0.25. The following table gives all block pairs at one, five, and ten neighbors."}
cross_domain_figure(cross_summary)
```

```{r cross-domain-agreement-table, echo = FALSE}
cross_summary |>
  summarise(
    k1 = median_overlap[k == 1L], k5 = median_overlap[k == 5L],
    k10 = median_overlap[k == 10L], .by = c(block_a, block_b)
  ) |>
  transmute(
    `Block A` = unname(block_labels[block_a]),
    `Block B` = unname(block_labels[block_b]), k1, k5, k10
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, col.names = c(
    "Block A", "Block B", "One neighbor", "Five neighbors", "Ten neighbors"
  ))
```

For Commercial and Industrial Designers, activities point to Fashion
Designers while software points to Graphic Designers. Essential-Level
ratings instead point to Landscape Architects. The nursing example also
changes with the domain:

```{r cross-domain-selected, echo = FALSE}
cross_selected |>
  summarise(
    `Nearest descriptions, including ties` = paste(neighbor_title, collapse = "; "),
    .by = c("occupation_title", "block")
  ) |>
  transmute(
    Occupation = occupation_title, Block = unname(block_labels[block]),
    `Nearest descriptions, including ties`
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

These are neighbors among published descriptions on a restricted support.
The absence of Accountants or Software Developers from this table follows
the suppression rule, not a claim that their skills or software cannot be
studied. The 894-code skill sensitivity is kept separately. No raw
activity, software or rating distance is treated as a common unit, and
none of these neighbors establishes an easy worker transition.

## When do differences disappear?

### Coarser labels can mechanically erase differences

Collapse the stylized activities into their invented broad groups, holding the
universe and activity mass fixed. In a real archive, use the published
DWA-to-IWA-to-GWA hierarchy instead of these demonstration labels.

```{r aggregation-sensitivity}
broad_profiles <- activity_profiles |>
  left_join(activity_labels, by = "item", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  summarise(weight = sum(weight), .by = c(occupation, broad_group)) |>
  rename(item = broad_group)
coarse_distances <- profile_distances(broad_profiles, universe) |>
  rename(broad_distance = distance)
resolution_comparison <- activity_distances |>
  rename(detailed_distance = distance) |>
  left_join(
    coarse_distances, by = c("occupation_a", "occupation_b"),
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  ) |>
  mutate(distance_lost = detailed_distance - broad_distance) |>
  arrange(desc(distance_lost), occupation_a, occupation_b)
resolution_comparison |>
  head(8) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

pair_ab <- resolution_comparison |>
  filter(occupation_a == "A", occupation_b == "B")
stopifnot(
  abs(pair_ab$detailed_distance - 1 / 3) < 1e-12,
  pair_ab$broad_distance == 0,
  all(resolution_comparison$distance_lost >= -1e-12)
)
```

In the stylized example, A and B differ in testing versus reporting, but both
have the same broad information/interaction mixture. Their distance disappears
**because the representation discards that distinction**, not because their
work has changed. With mass-preserving grouping, total variation cannot
increase. That is a mathematical property of grouping, so a drop in distance is
guaranteed and is not itself a finding. Re-binarizing the broad groups or
re-estimating IDF changes additional assumptions, so assess those changes
separately.

The same mass-preserving coarsening can be run on the full archive. The next
table uses the published hierarchy, holds the occupation universe fixed, and
does not refit IDF or re-binarize parent activities. Read it with care: at the
detailed grain, 371,633 of 425,503 occupation pairs (87.3 percent) share no
DWA, and the mean pairwise distance is 0.987. A statistic that starts this
close to its ceiling has little room to move, and by itself it does not show
how distinctive occupations are. The null reference below makes that concrete.

```{r observed-resolution}
observed_resolution |>
  mutate(grain = c("Detailed activities", "Intermediate activities",
                   "Generalized activities")) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The reduction measures what grouping activity labels discards from a
near-saturated statistic. It is not evidence that workers' actual jobs have
converged over time.

### An information-loss budget for coarsening

The information-loss budget asks how much information about occupation identity
survives when activity labels are grouped. This borrows the
relevance-target idea from the information bottleneck of Tishby, Pereira, and
Bialek: judge a compression by how much information it retains about a target
variable. We do not fit the bottleneck algorithm. The hierarchy is fixed in
advance by O&#42;NET.

Draw an occupation \(O\) uniformly from the \(N\) covered occupations. Then
draw a detailed activity \(D\) from that occupation's profile shares
\(p_{od}\). The mixture is the mean profile, **not** the document-frequency
ratio:

\[
q_d = \frac{1}{N}\sum_o p_{od}
\]
\[
I(O;D) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_o\sum_d p_{od}\log_2\frac{p_{od}}{q_d}.
\]

\(I(O;D)\) is the mean Kullback-Leibler divergence, in bits, between each
occupation's profile and the mean profile. It lies between zero and
\(\log_2 N\). Aggregating the original mass through the fixed
DWA-to-IWA-to-GWA hierarchy gives \(I(O;\text{IWA})\) and \(I(O;\text{GWA})\).
By the data-processing inequality,

\[
I(O;D) \ge I(O;\text{IWA}) \ge I(O;\text{GWA}).
\]

The decrease is guaranteed, so the informative quantities are its size, how it
splits across hierarchy groups, and the retained percentage relative to the
detailed bits. Losses by parent group add up exactly to the total bits
discarded between the detailed and generalized grains.

**This is accounting, not a new metric.** When every occupation has the same
number \(n\) of binary activities, \(p_{od}=1/n\) and
\(q_d = df_d/(nN)\), so each occupation's divergence in bits equals its mean
IDF divided by \(\ln 2\). Unequal profile sizes break that equality. The new
contribution is the bookkeeping of what each grouping level discards. It is not
a new uniqueness score and it is not a validated correction for profile size.

```{r information-values, include = FALSE}
fmt_bits <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
stopifnot(
  identical(information_summary$grain,
            c("dwa_element_id", "iwa_element_id", "gwa_element_id")),
  all(c("gwa_element_id", "gwa_element_name", "n_dwas", "mixture_mass",
        "lost_bits", "conditional_lost_bits") %in% names(information_loss)),
  abs(sum(information_loss$lost_bits) -
        information_summary$lost_from_dwa_bits[[3]]) < 1e-8
)
info_dwa <- information_summary$information_bits[[1]]
info_iwa <- information_summary$information_bits[[2]]
info_gwa <- information_summary$information_bits[[3]]
info_max <- log2(information_summary$n_occupations[[1]])
```

```{r information-table, echo = FALSE}
information_summary |>
  mutate(grain = c("Detailed (DWA)", "Intermediate (IWA)", "Generalized (GWA)")) |>
  select(
    grain, n_labels_with_positive_mass, information_bits,
    lost_from_dwa_bits, retained_dwa_percent
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, col.names = c(
    "Grain", "Labels with mass", "Information (bits)",
    "Lost from DWA (bits)", "Retained (% of DWA bits)"
  ))
```

```{r information-text, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat(sprintf(
  paste0(
    "Detailed activities carry %s bits of the at most %s bits that could ",
    "identify one of %d occupations. Intermediate groups retain %s bits ",
    "(%.1f percent of the detailed total) and generalized groups retain %s ",
    "bits (%.1f percent), a loss of %s bits. The retained percentages use ",
    "the detailed bits as the denominator.\n"
  ),
  fmt_bits(info_dwa), fmt_bits(info_max),
  information_summary$n_occupations[[1]],
  fmt_bits(info_iwa), information_summary$retained_dwa_percent[[2]],
  fmt_bits(info_gwa), information_summary$retained_dwa_percent[[3]],
  fmt_bits(information_summary$lost_from_dwa_bits[[3]])
))
```

```{r figure-information, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Real O*NET 30.3 information budget: bits of occupation identity carried by activity labels at each grain, with the percentage of detailed bits retained.", fig.alt = "Bar chart of information in bits at the detailed, intermediate, and generalized activity grains: about 6.39, 3.95, and 1.67 bits, which is 100, 61.9, and 26.1 percent of the detailed bits. The table above gives the exact values."}
audit_figures$information
```

```{r figure-loss, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Real O*NET 30.3: eight generalized-activity groups with the largest bits discarded when detailed activities are grouped. Large losses can reflect large group mass.", fig.alt = "Bar chart of discarded bits for the eight generalized work activity groups with the largest losses. The group losses across all 41 groups sum to about 4.72 bits discarded between the detailed and generalized grains. The table below gives the eight largest groups; the bundled information-loss CSV contains all 41."}
audit_figures$loss
```

```{r loss-table, echo = FALSE}
information_loss |>
  slice_max(lost_bits, n = 8, with_ties = TRUE) |>
  select(all_of(c(
    "gwa_element_name", "n_dwas", "mixture_mass",
    "lost_bits", "conditional_lost_bits"
  ))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4, col.names = c(
    "Generalized activity group", "DWAs", "Share of mean profile",
    "Lost bits", "Lost bits per unit of mass"
  ))
```

The figure and table show the eight largest groups. The bundled
`information-loss.csv` contains results for all 41 groups.

A group's weighted loss rises with its share of the mean profile
(`mixture_mass`), so a large group can top the table simply because it is
large. The conditional loss, which divides by that mass, shows the loss per
unit of mass. The budget is not classification accuracy, and it does not
measure semantic richness, difficulty, AI exposure, or whether jobs are
converging. It describes how much a given set of labels can say about occupation
identity under this sampling model.

### Does the published GWA grouping discard more than size alone?

This diagnostic randomly assigns the 2,083 DWA labels to 41 groups while
preserving the observed number of DWA labels in each group. The DWA-to-
occupation profiles stay fixed. The random assignments deliberately break the
published semantic groupings and IWA nesting, so this is a size-preserving
partition reference, not an economic null model or an inferential test.

```{r figure-random-hierarchy, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Observed generalized-activity grouping compared with 200 random assignments that preserve the number of detailed activities per group.", fig.alt = "Histogram of information about occupation identity under 200 random DWA group assignments that preserve the observed group sizes. A teal vertical line marks the observed O*NET GWA grouping."}
audit_figures$random_hierarchy
```

The observed generalized grouping carries `r fmt_bits(info_gwa)` bits. The
5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles of the random-partition reference are
`r paste(fmt_bits(stats::quantile(random_hierarchy$information_bits, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))), collapse = ", ")`
bits. `r sum(random_hierarchy$information_bits <= info_gwa)` of the
`r nrow(random_hierarchy)` assignments have information no greater than the
observed grouping. This comparison isolates group size under the specified
uniform assignment scheme; it does not establish that the O&#42;NET hierarchy
is uniquely meaningful or that occupations form natural families.

### Is the distance more than a fixed-margin shuffle would give?

A fixed-margin reference helps judge the near-ceiling numbers above. The
Curveball algorithm of Strona and colleagues swaps activities between two
occupations while preserving **each occupation's number of DWAs and each DWA's
frequency exactly**. The reference here uses twenty separately restarted chains,
each starting from the observed activity sets. Each chain attempts \(20N\)
trades, and attempted no-op trades count. All chains are distinct pseudorandom
draws under one seed, 20261025. The resulting sets are aggregated through the
same fixed hierarchy. Draw 0 is the observed archive, and draws 1 to 20 are the
reference draws.

```{r null-table, echo = FALSE}
stopifnot(all(c("draw", "grain", "mean_pair_distance",
                "median_nearest_distance") %in% names(null_summary)))
null_summary |>
  mutate(
    source = ifelse(draw == 0L, "Observed", "Reference draws"),
    grain = factor(
      grain, levels = c("dwa_element_id", "iwa_element_id", "gwa_element_id"),
      labels = c("DWA", "IWA", "GWA")
    )
  ) |>
  summarise(
    mean_pair_min = min(mean_pair_distance),
    mean_pair_max = max(mean_pair_distance),
    nearest_min = min(median_nearest_distance),
    nearest_max = max(median_nearest_distance),
    n_draws = n(),
    .by = c(source, grain)
  ) |>
  arrange(grain, source) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4, col.names = c(
    "Source", "Grain", "Mean pair min", "Mean pair max",
    "Median nearest min", "Median nearest max", "Draws"
  ))
```

```{r figure-null, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Real O*NET 30.3 against fixed-margin Curveball reference draws: pairwise and nearest-neighbor distance at each grain.", fig.alt = "Chart comparing observed values with twenty fixed-margin reference draws at each grain. The mean pairwise distance at the detailed grain is about 0.987 observed and about 0.986 in the reference draws, a small absolute difference with the observed value slightly above all twenty endpoints. At the generalized grain the observed mean pairwise distance is higher (0.716 against 0.615 to 0.625) while the median nearest-neighbor distance is lower. The median nearest-neighbor distance at the detailed grain is about 0.59 observed against about 0.86 in the reference draws. The table above gives the exact minimum and maximum values."}
audit_figures$null
```

At the detailed grain, the observed mean pairwise distance is
`r sprintf("%.4f", null_summary$mean_pair_distance[null_summary$grain == "dwa_element_id" & null_summary$draw == 0L])`,
compared with `r sprintf("%.4f to %.4f", min(null_summary$mean_pair_distance[null_summary$grain == "dwa_element_id" & null_summary$draw > 0L]), max(null_summary$mean_pair_distance[null_summary$grain == "dwa_element_id" & null_summary$draw > 0L]))`
across the twenty reference draws. This absolute difference is small. At the
generalized grain, the observed mean pairwise distance is
`r sprintf("%.4f", null_summary$mean_pair_distance[null_summary$grain == "gwa_element_id" & null_summary$draw == 0L])`,
compared with `r sprintf("%.4f to %.4f", min(null_summary$mean_pair_distance[null_summary$grain == "gwa_element_id" & null_summary$draw > 0L]), max(null_summary$mean_pair_distance[null_summary$grain == "gwa_element_id" & null_summary$draw > 0L]))`.
The observed median nearest distance at the detailed grain is
`r sprintf("%.4f", null_summary$median_nearest_distance[null_summary$grain == "dwa_element_id" & null_summary$draw == 0L])`,
compared with `r sprintf("%.4f to %.4f", min(null_summary$median_nearest_distance[null_summary$grain == "dwa_element_id" & null_summary$draw > 0L]), max(null_summary$median_nearest_distance[null_summary$grain == "dwa_element_id" & null_summary$draw > 0L]))`
across the reference draws. In this finite reference, observed mean pairwise
distances are above, and median nearest distances below, the corresponding
reference ranges at each grain. This is a descriptive comparison, not an
inferential test.
The twenty finite endpoints are not certified as uniform draws, and the
minimum-to-maximum range is not a confidence interval. The shuffled sets are
synthetic activity bundles, not economic counterfactuals. Because mixing is not
certified, the gap is not a proof of a statistical difference. It also does not
prove that the archive has, or lacks, economic structure.

### Similarity can also increase without work converging

| Change in analysis | Why a gap might shrink | Diagnostic |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Replace detailed tasks with broad activities | Distinct tasks acquire the same label | Hold weights fixed and compare DWA, IWA, and GWA distances |
| Keep only common skills | Shared descriptors crowd out specialized knowledge | Report domain-specific distances and dropped-feature coverage |
| Normalize each profile | Absolute requirement levels disappear | Retain raw scale-level gaps |
| Average occupations into industries | Different occupational mixtures yield similar means | Separate within-occupation profiles from employment composition |
| Change the reference universe or refit IDF | Rarity changes even if no activity changes | Score both samples with the same reference IDF |
| Drop missing or suppressed observations | The most distinctive observations may leave the sample | Show exclusions and common-support results |
| Compare adjacent database releases | Copied records can look stable without fresh measurement | Use source dates, resurvey indicators, and taxonomy seam flags |

For industry comparisons, "common across occupations" is not "common among
workers." Use employment weights to calculate a separate worker-weighted
prevalence, and show coverage and the SOC bridge. Do not describe linked task
counts or Relevance ratings as worker time shares. An industry-level result
also needs an occupation-by-industry employment panel, not just national
occupational employment.

For changes over time, freeze a baseline IDF to measure changes in occupational
profiles on a common scale. Refit IDF separately as a sensitivity analysis of
changing rarity. Keep taxonomy and vocabulary mappings visible. See
[Resurvey Cycles and Content Change](resurvey-and-content-change.html) and
[Change Decomposition](within-between-decomposition.html). A descriptive
convergence result does not identify whether technology, training, regulation,
or organizational change caused it. Those explanations need additional
outcomes, timing, and an identification strategy.

## Run the analysis on a local archive

The following is deliberately **not evaluated** during article builds. Download
the public 30.3 text archive separately and point `archive_path` at the ZIP or
its extracted directory. No API key is required. Keep the source receipt and
digest with the analysis. The tables used here are not the entire published
occupation taxonomy, so define the analytic universe from documented coverage.

```{r full-archive, eval = FALSE}
archive_path <- "path/to/db_30_3_text.zip"
full_tasks <- onet_archive_read(
  "30.3", "Task Statements", path = archive_path
)
full_links <- onet_archive_read(
  "30.3", "Tasks to DWAs", path = archive_path
)
full_hierarchy <- onet_archive_reference(
  "30.3", "GWAs to IWAs to DWAs", path = archive_path
)
occupation_names <- onet_archive_read(
  "30.3", "Occupation Data", path = archive_path
) |>
  distinct(onet_soc_code, title)
full_names <- full_hierarchy |>
  distinct(dwa_element_id, dwa_element_name)

# Baseline: any linked task, including Supplemental tasks.
# Optional Core-only sensitivity: uncomment this filter and replace `full_links`
# with `core_links` below. This shrinks the occupation universe, so recalculate
# prevalence and all rankings within the reduced universe.
# core_task_keys <- full_tasks |>
#   filter(task_type == "Core") |>
#   distinct(onet_soc_code, task_id)
# core_links <- full_links |>
#   semi_join(core_task_keys, by = c("onet_soc_code", "task_id"))
full_profiles <- full_links |>
  distinct(onet_soc_code, dwa_element_id) |>
  transmute(occupation = onet_soc_code, item = dwa_element_id, weight = 1)
full_universe <- sort(unique(full_profiles$occupation))
task_coverage <- full_tasks |>
  distinct(onet_soc_code, task_id) |>
  left_join(
    full_links |>
      distinct(onet_soc_code, task_id) |>
      mutate(has_dwa = TRUE),
    by = c("onet_soc_code", "task_id"),
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    n_tasks = n(), linked_tasks = sum(!is.na(has_dwa)),
    .by = onet_soc_code
  )
print(task_coverage)
print(anti_join(
  full_tasks |> distinct(onet_soc_code),
  full_profiles |> distinct(onet_soc_code = occupation),
  by = "onet_soc_code"
))
full_scores <- profile_tfidf(full_profiles, full_universe)
full_scores |>
  distinct(item, n_occupations, prevalence, idf) |>
  left_join(
    full_names, by = c("item" = "dwa_element_id"),
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(prevalence), item) |>
  print(n = 20)
full_scores |>
  summarise(mean_idf = sum(tf_idf), .by = occupation) |>
  left_join(
    occupation_names, by = c("occupation" = "onet_soc_code"),
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_idf), occupation) |>
  print(n = 20)

experience <- onet_archive_read(
  "30.3", "Training and Experience", path = archive_path
)
experience_categories <- onet_archive_reference(
  "30.3", "Training and Experience Categories", path = archive_path
)
# Audit missing/suppressed values and category completeness before normalization.
experience |>
  filter(scale_id == "RW") |>
  select(onet_soc_code, element_id, scale_id, category, data_value,
         recommend_suppress) |>
  left_join(
    experience_categories |>
      select(element_id, scale_id, category, category_description),
    by = c("element_id", "scale_id", "category"),
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  )
```

For a production analysis, retain a manifest with release, source digest,
taxonomy, inclusion rule, mapping grain, weight scale, suppression treatment,
occupation universe, and IDF reference. Check coverage separately for each
domain, then use common support for cross-domain comparisons. In rating
tables, absence means missing unless you have evidence it means zero.

The full-archive ranking above is conditional on its vocabulary, comparison
universe, and weighting decisions. Skills and software have separate empirical
results; education, experience and knowledge do not acquire a national ranking
from these comparisons.

### Reproduce the bundled snapshot

The snapshot was generated on `r snapshot$snapshot_date` from
[`r snapshot$source_url`](`r snapshot$source_url`).
The archive SHA-256 is:

```{r snapshot-digest, echo = FALSE}
cat(snapshot$source_sha256, "\n")
```

From a source checkout with the current package installed, run these three
commands, each with the same local ZIP argument:

```
Rscript data-raw/occupational-distinctiveness.R path/to/db_30_3_text.zip
Rscript data-raw/occupational-information.R path/to/db_30_3_text.zip
Rscript data-raw/occupational-null.R path/to/db_30_3_text.zip
```

They regenerate the derived CSVs under
`inst/extdata/occupational-distinctiveness/`. The generators record coverage and
provenance, check task-link integrity and mass-preserving coarsening, and check
the archive digest. The `task-inventory.csv` file carries task-vintage and
inventory metadata. The raw archive is not bundled. Source date and identifier
changes across releases still require separate review.

For the employment, skills and common-support extensions, run:

```
Rscript data-raw\occupational-skills.R path\to\db_30_3_text.zip
Rscript data-raw\occupational-employment.R path\to\db_30_3_text.zip path\to\oesm25nat.zip path\to\occupation_definitions_m2025.xlsx
Rscript data-raw\occupational-cross-domain.R path\to\db_30_3_text.zip
```

The employment script checks all three input digests. The national ZIP comes
from the [BLS OEWS tables page](https://www.bls.gov/oes/tables.htm); the
[May 2025 definitions workbook](https://www.bls.gov/oes/occupation_definitions_m2025.xlsx)
provides the combined-cell constituents. BLS may reject scripted downloads.
The input receipts record how the pinned bytes were retrieved.
The extension README and decision ledger retain source gaps, including the
unverified ownership-code interpretation and unread Survey Methods PDF.
Neither an ownership comparison nor propagation of OEWS sampling error is
claimed.

The largest derived tables use lossless gzip compression (`.csv.gz`).
Base R reads them with `read.csv()`; compression changes storage, not the rows
or the analysis.

## Sources and scope

This article includes information derived from the
[O&#42;NET 30.3 Database](https://www.onetcenter.org/db_releases.html) by the
U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration (USDOL/ETA),
used under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
O&#42;NET is a trademark of USDOL/ETA. onet2r has modified the information by
calculating the frequencies, scores, distances, information-loss accounting,
fixed-margin randomizations, and coverage summaries described
above. USDOL/ETA has not approved, endorsed, or tested these modifications.

The data representations above follow the O&#42;NET Resource Center's
[Tasks to DWAs dictionary](https://www.onetcenter.org/dictionary/30.3/excel/tasks_to_dwas.html),
[activity hierarchy](https://www.onetcenter.org/dictionary/30.3/excel/gwas_to_iwas_to_dwas.html),
[Essential Skills dictionary](https://www.onetcenter.org/dictionary/30.3/excel/essential_skills.html),
[Transferable Skills dictionary](https://www.onetcenter.org/dictionary/30.3/excel/transferable_skills.html),
[scale definitions](https://www.onetcenter.org/dictionary/30.3/excel/scales_reference.html),
[Training and Experience dictionary](https://www.onetcenter.org/dictionary/30.3/excel/training_and_experience.html),
and [experience category definitions](https://www.onetcenter.org/dictionary/30.3/excel/training_and_experience_categories.html).
Verified schema facts are recorded in `docs/DATA_NOTES.md`.

TF-IDF is adapted from information retrieval. For the underlying distinction
between term frequency and document frequency, see Manning, Raghavan, and
Schuetze, *Introduction to Information Retrieval*, section 6.2,
[Term frequency and weighting](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/term-frequency-and-weighting-1.html).
The occupation-level summary, distances, and weighting rules here are explicit
analytical choices, not measures validated by that reference.

The information-loss budget borrows the relevance-target idea from Tishby,
Pereira, and Bialek, [The information bottleneck method](https://arxiv.org/html/physics/0004057v1).
We do not fit the bottleneck algorithm, and that reference does not validate
the budget as a measure of occupational distinctiveness. The fixed-margin
reference uses the Curveball algorithm: Strona et al. (2014), "A fast and
unbiased procedure to randomize ecological binary matrices with fixed row and
column totals," *Nature Communications* 5:4114,
[doi:10.1038/ncomms5114](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms5114).
